cards.text: The fighting is over, and Mordecai, the Jew who raised Queen Esther (Esther 2:7), picks up a pen. He records everything and sends letters to all the Jews in every province of King Xerxes, near AND far. Friend, that is a LOT of letters, and my mustache is cramping just thinking about it.

cards.question: What are Mordecai's letters setting up for the Jews?

answers.text: A new tax for the palace

cards.question: Mordecai sets the celebration on the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the month of ___.

cards.text: Mordecai explains why these days get a party: they're the days the Jews gained rest from their enemies. Friend, I had YEARS of rest in a junk drawer, and trust me, it was NOT this kind.

cards.question: Mordecai also writes about the Jews' sorrow in this month. What happened to it?
Mordecai writes that these days of feasting and joy include sending gifts to one another and to the poor.
Mordecai's letters arrive, and the Jews refuse to keep the custom they had started.

cards.text: Now the text looks back at how this all started. Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted to destroy them.

cards.question: Haman cast something in his plan to crush the Jews. What is it called?

cards.text: But when it came before King Xerxes, he gave a command by letter. Haman built a wicked scheme against the Jews, and now we find out where it lands.

cards.question: What did King Xerxes command about Haman's wicked scheme against the Jews?

answers.text: It would come back on Haman's own head
It would be quietly forgotten by the court
It would go ahead exactly as planned

cards.text: The king commands that Haman and his sons be hanged on the gallows. All that plotting, friend, and the scheme lands right back where it started.

cards.question: These days of celebration get their name from something in Haman's plot. What are they named after?

cards.text: So these days are called Purim, from the word Pur, and because of the letter and everything they had seen and lived through, the Jews bind themselves to keep them. Friend, that's a reminder set to repeat every year, and NOBODY is hitting snooze.

cards.question: The Jews bind themselves to celebrate these two days at the appointed time every year. Who else does it cover?

answers.text: Their descendants and all who join them
Their servants and the king's officials
The Persians and all their neighbors

cards.question: The plan is for the days of Purim to fade from memory once the danger is long past.

cards.text: Now Queen Esther, daughter of Abihail, picks up a pen too. She and Mordecai the Jew write with full authority to confirm this second letter about Purim.

cards.question: Mordecai sends letters to all the Jews in the 127 provinces of Xerxes's kingdom. What kind of words fill those letters?
The letters confirm the days of Purim, just as Mordecai and Queen Esther had set them up. The two of them had also committed themselves and their descendants to the times of ___ and lamentation.

cards.text: Esther's decree confirms the rules about Purim, and they're written into the record. Friend, nobody is sliding THAT paper to the back of a junk drawer, and believe me, I'd know.
Meanwhile King Xerxes puts tribute on the whole land, all the way to its farthest shores. And Mordecai? Somebody's been taking notes on him.

cards.question: Mordecai's powerful accomplishments, and how high the king raised him, are all written down. Where?

answers.text: The Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Media and Persia
The Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel
The Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah

cards.question: How high does Mordecai the Jew rank in the kingdom of Xerxes?
With all that power, Mordecai seeks the good of his people and speaks peace to all his countrymen.

cards.text: Preeminent among the Jews and highly favored by his many kinsmen. Friend, THAT is how you handle a promotion, because somebody hands ME a new oven mitt and I'm unbearable for a week.
